stem: When was the new Enfield Rifle with greased cartridges introduced in the British Indian Army?
expl: In December, 1856, the government decided to replace the old Brown Bess musket with the new Enfield rifle. Training for these rifles was to be given at Dum Dum, Ambala and Sialkot. These rifles used greased cartridges, which were said to be coated with the fat of cows and pigs. In this rifle, the upper part of the cartridge had to be bitten off with the mouth. In January, 1857, a rumour spread in the Bengal Army that the greased cartridges contained the fat of cows and pigs. The military officers denied it immediately without proper investigation. But the soldiers became convinced that the use of such cartridges was a deliberate attempt to corrupt their religion, and this became the immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857.

expl: The incident of 24 April, 1857 at Meerut proved to be a milestone in the history of India’s freedom struggle. Colonel Carmichael Smyth ordered that greased cartridges be issued to Indian soldiers, which had to be opened with the mouth. Angered by this, 85 out of 90 soldiers of the 3rd Bengal Native Cavalry / 3rd Regiment of Light Cavalry revolted against these cartridges. On 9 May, 1857, these rebel soldiers were court-martialled at the Meerut parade ground. Enraged by this action, they revolted at Meerut on 10 May, 1857 and sounded the bugle of the first war of independence, i.e., the Revolt of 1857.

expl: The Revolt of 1857 spread over a very large area and received wide popular support. Even so, it could not engulf the whole country or all sections and classes of Indian society. It did not spread to South India and to most parts of Eastern and Western India. Most rulers of the Indian princely states and the big zamindars were self-seeking and, frightened of British power, did not join the revolt. On the contrary, the Scindia of Gwalior, the Holkar of Indore, the Nizam of Hyderabad, the Maharaja of Jodhpur, the Sikh rulers of Patiala, Nabha and Jind, other Sikh chiefs of Punjab, the Maharaja of Kashmir, and many other chiefs and big zamindars actively helped the British in suppressing the revolt. Governor-General Canning later remarked that these rulers “acted like a dam before the storm; otherwise the storm would have swept us away in a single wave.” Traders and the educated class held meetings in Calcutta and Bombay and appealed to help the British. Most people of the upper and middle classes were critics of the rebels. Many talukdars (big zamindars) of Awadh who had joined the revolt withdrew from it after receiving an assurance from the British that their estates would be restored. In rural attacks, the main targets were moneylenders; therefore, they naturally became enemies of the revolt. Indians with modern education also did not support the revolt. The educated Indians wanted to remove the backwardness of the country. They were wrongly convinced that the British would help them in completing these tasks of modernization.

stem: What was the main cause of the failure of the revolt of 1857?

options.label: b

options.label: c
options.text: Its effect was within a limited area

expl: The main reason for the failure of the Revolt of 1857 was the lack of a common plan and a central organization. No spirit of organization was seen among the rebel leaders. The 82-year-old Bahadur Shah was weak, and his call to various chiefs was not sufficient. The rebels certainly showed bravery and appeared determined to destroy the government, but they completely lacked a planned and unified programme to do so. They also lacked discipline. At times, they behaved like a rioting mob rather than a disciplined army. Except for a shared hatred towards foreign rule, there was no other binding link among the leaders. After uprooting British authority from a particular region, they did not even know what kind of political power or institutions should be established in its place. They lacked a future-oriented programme, coherent ideology, political perspective, or a clear vision of a future society and economy.

stem: When did Queen Victoria declare the taking over of Indian administration under the British Crown?
expl: After the suppression of the Revolt of 1857, on 1 November, 1858, Queen Victoria declared that Indian administration would be taken under the control of the British Crown. stem: Which one of the following commissions is associated with the Army Reorganization after the suppression of the Revolt of 1857?
expl: After the suppression of the Revolt of 1857, the British government appointed the Peel Commission for the reorganization of the Indian army. It recommended adopting the principle of keeping different castes and communities mixed within the regiments. The number of European soldiers, which was 45,000 before 1857, was increased to 65,000, and the number of Indian soldiers was reduced from 238,000 to 140,000. In Bengal, the ratio of European soldiers to Indian soldiers was kept at 1:2, whereas in Madras and Bombay this ratio was kept at 1:3.

expl: The Indigo Revolt began from Govindpur village in Nadia district of Bengal. Under the leadership of two former employees of an indigo planter—Digambar Biswas and Vishnu Biswas (Vishnucharan Biswas)—the peasants united there and stopped cultivating indigo. This was the most widespread and militant revolt in the history of indigo movements in terms of demands. The Indigo Revolt of Bengal was the peasants’ direct struggle against exploitation. The cultivators of Bengal who wanted to grow rice in their fields were forced by European indigo planters to cultivate indigo. Those who refused indigo cultivation had to face the oppressive machinery of the planters. In March 1859, thousands of raiyats in Bengal refused to cultivate indigo. As the revolt spread, the raiyats also refused to pay rent to the planters. By 1860, the indigo movement spread to Nadia, Pabna, Khulna, Dhaka, Malda, Dinajpur, etc. Due to the unity of the peasants, by 1860 almost all indigo factories in Bengal were closed. The intellectual class of Bengal expressed support for this revolt through newspaper articles and public meetings. The editor of “Hindu Patriot,” Harishchandra Mukherjee, played a special role in it. The atrocities of indigo planters were vividly portrayed by Dinabandhu Mitra in his play “Neel Darpan.”

stem: Who founded the ‘Pagal Panth’?
expl: The Pagal Panth was a semi-religious sect initiated by Karam/ Karim Shah. In reality, it was a revolt associated with the Garo tribe. The Pagalpanthi revolt mainly spread in the Sherpur and Mymensingh regions of Bengal (located in present-day Bangladesh). stem: Trace the tribe that rebelled against Britishers because human sacrifice system was banned –
expl: The Khond tribal people lived in a vast hilly belt stretching from Tamil Nadu to Bengal and Central India. Because it was a hilly region, they were largely independent. They revolted against the British during 1846–1855 (the movement continued even before and after this period; this phase is mainly associated with the leadership of Chakra Bisoi) in the name of a young king. The main causes of the revolt were the British government’s attempts to ban human sacrifice (Meriah), the imposition of new taxes, and the entry of zamindars and moneylenders into many areas, which caused immense suffering to the tribals. The British formed a Meriah Agency, against which the Khonds rebelled.

In Western Punjab, the Kuka Movement was started in the 1840s by Bhagat Jawahar Mal, who was mainly known as Sian Sahib. His objective was to remove the evils and superstitions prevalent in Sikhism and purify this religion. However, later it turned into a political movement, led by Ram Singh. In 1872, the leader of this movement, Ram Singh, was exiled to Rangoon (Myanmar), and he died in Magui (Myanmar) in 1885.

expl: The movement of the Moplah (Mappila) tenants of Malabar in the Kerala province was mainly related to rent and eviction. The zamindars evicted them from the land whenever they wished and collected arbitrary rent as they pleased. The Khilafat Movement was also taking root. The situation became such that it was difficult to differentiate between meetings of the Khilafat Movement and those of the tenants. In this way, both movements merged into each other.

expl: The Tebhaga Movement (1946–47) was a famous peasant movement of Bengal. Under it, peasants began a struggle to reduce the rent rate to one-third in accordance with the recommendations of the ‘Floud Commission’. This movement, fought under the leadership of the Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha (BPKS), was a movement of sharecroppers against the jotedars.

expl: In the 1940s, the Tebhaga Movement began in Bengal. At that time, farmers had to give half the share to the sharecroppers, whereas the peasants ran the Tebhaga Movement to give only one-third of the crop share.
